The Story of Kadarping

I bow to the Arhants, the word of Jina, and the gurus, and I write the story of Kadarping, who fell from the vow of contentment with one's own wife.

In the famous city of Kapilya, there ruled a wise and virtuous king named Narsingh. He governed with justice, and his people loved him dearly. The royal minister was Sumati, whose wife was Dhanshri, and they had a son named Kadarping. Kadarping's conduct was not good — he was deeply lustful.

In the same city lived a merchant named Kuberadatt, a very righteous man devoted to worship and religious celebrations. His wife, Priyangsundari, was gentle, virtuous, and very beautiful.

One day Kadarping saw Priyangsundari going somewhere, and upon beholding her beauty, his mind became restless. Wherever he looked, he saw only her. Nothing else pleased him. Lust robbed him of all reason. He barely managed to reach home in that distraught state. Seeing him so agitated, his mother was deeply worried and asked, "Kadar, why has your condition changed so suddenly? You left home perfectly well — what has happened?" Kadarping, without thought or shame, blurted out that if he could somehow obtain Kuberadatt's wife, he could live; otherwise, death was certain.

The sages say: cursed are those blinded by lust, who lose all sense of shame and fear and cannot distinguish right from wrong. Poor Dhanshri was stunned by her son's shamelessness. She said nothing and went straight to her husband to tell him everything. Sumati was a royal minister and a wise man. He should have tried to turn his son away from sin. Instead, fearing that his son might die, he lent his hand to the sinful act. Truly, when the time of destruction approaches, even the intellect turns perverse.

Sumati devised a plan. He invited Kuberadatt to the palace on some pretext and detained him there. Meanwhile, Kadarping went to Priyangsundari's house. But Priyangsundari was a woman of great virtue and recognised the intruder at once. She firmly refused him and drove him away with sharp words, declaring her devotion to her husband and her commitment to chastity. Kadarping slunk away in shame.

When the truth came to light, King Narsingh was furious. He summoned Sumati and Kadarping and rebuked them severely. A minister who aids his son's lust instead of correcting him is no better than the sinner himself. Both were punished, and Kadarping's name became a byword for disgrace. The merchant Kuberadatt and his wife Priyangsundari, meanwhile, were honoured for their virtue and fidelity.

This story teaches that lust is a fire that consumes the one who harbours it. It blinds reason, destroys shame, and leads to actions that bring lasting disgrace. And parents who enable their children's sins rather than correcting them share in the guilt. True love for a child means guiding them away from sin, not helping them sink deeper into it.
